q: Who usually performs user acceptance testing?
why: UAT confirms the solution meets business needs, so business users perform it.

q: Which test checks that a new change didn't break existing functionality?
why: Regression testing re-runs earlier tests to catch unintended side effects.

q: Checking that the ledger feed correctly reaches the matching engine is which test level?
why: Integration testing verifies that components or systems work together.

q: Old and new systems process the same data and their results are compared. This is…
why: Parallel runs are common in finance to prove the new system gives identical results.

q: What is the purpose of a smoke test?
options: Check that basic functions work well enough to continue testing
why: A smoke test is a quick build-verification check.

q: Testing behavior without looking at the code is called…
why: Black-box testing focuses on inputs and outputs. BAs and UAT testers work this way.

q: What is the difference between a test scenario and a test case?
options: A scenario says what to test; a test case gives detailed steps, data and expected results
A test case is higher level than a scenario
Scenarios are only for performance testing
why: Scenarios are high level; test cases are detailed and repeatable.

q: A rule escalates breaks older than 30 days. Boundary value analysis suggests testing…
why: Test just below, at and just above the boundary, where defects cluster.

q: Grouping inputs that should behave the same way and testing one from each group is…
why: Equivalence partitioning reduces the number of tests while keeping coverage.

q: Testing with a blank reference, a future date, or an unauthorized user is…
why: Negative testing checks how the system handles invalid input or misuse.

q: Why should every test case reference a requirement ID?
why: Linking tests to requirements supports the RTM and shows coverage.

q: Which is a typical UAT entry criterion?
options: System testing complete with no open critical defects
The product is live in production
why: UAT starts after system testing, when the environment and data are ready.

q: What should UAT scenarios be based on?
options: Real business work and realistic data
why: UAT tests whether the business can do its real job with the solution.

q: What formally ends UAT?
options: Business sign-off when exit criteria are met
why: UAT ends with formal acceptance by the business owner.

q: Testing done by a limited group of real customers in their own environment is…
why: Alpha is in-house; beta is with real users outside.

q: A retest of a 'fixed' defect fails. What status does it move to?
why: Failed retests reopen the defect.

q: A defect is valid but the team agrees to fix it in a later release. Its status is…
why: Deferred defects are valid but scheduled for later.

q: Developers mark a defect 'works as designed', but users still think it's wrong. What does this often indicate?
options: A requirements gap the BA should investigate
why: It often means the requirement didn't capture the real need. The BA may raise a change request.

q: Which defect title is most useful?
options: Approve button does nothing for matches over 10,000 AUD
why: Specific titles help triage and reproduction.

q: Severity describes ___ and priority describes ___.
options: who found it; who fixes it
why: Severity is how bad the defect is; priority is how soon it must be fixed.

q: The company logo is wrong on the client login page. Which classification is most likely?
why: It's cosmetic (low impact) but visible to clients, so it is urgent.

q: A crash in a yearly report that won't be used until next quarter is likely…
why: A crash is high impact, but there is time before it matters.

q: What does a defect triage meeting decide?
options: Validity, severity, priority, owner and when to fix each defect
why: Triage reviews new defects and agrees actions.

q: A minute-by-minute runbook for switching to the new solution is the…
why: The cutover plan sequences every go-live step with owners and checkpoints.

q: Which deployment strategy switches all users at once?
why: Big bang is simple but risky.

q: What is hypercare?
why: Hypercare provides extra support and monitoring before handover to BAU.

q: What should a rollback plan include?
options: Clear criteria for when to roll back and steps to return to the old state
why: Rollback criteria remove guesswork under pressure.

q: Rolling out to one country at a time is which strategy?
why: Phased rollouts reduce risk by limiting each step's scope.

q: In ITIL, what is the difference between an incident and a problem?
options: An incident is a service interruption; a problem is its underlying cause
A problem is smaller than an incident
why: Incident management restores service; problem management removes root causes.

q: 190 of 200 cases were resolved within SLA. What is SLA compliance?
Which is a good example of an SLA?
options: All breaks investigated within 2 business days
why: SLAs are specific, measurable commitments.

q: Which feature is most important in good exception handling?
options: Clear reason codes, owners, time limits and an escalation path
Handling them only at year end
Letting each analyst decide their own method
why: Structured handling makes exceptions consistent, timely and auditable.

q: How should case notes be written?
options: Clear, factual and neutral, so someone else can understand them later
As briefly as possible, even if unclear
why: Neutral, factual documentation supports audit, handover and fair decisions.

q: A routine user request such as new system access is called a…
why: ITIL distinguishes routine service requests from incidents.
